analysis.one_liner: Requires lead-paint hazard testing and cleanup in federally assisted housing where young children live.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a lead-hazard inspection of federally assisted housing generally happens only after a child has already been diagnosed with lead poisoning. This bill would have flipped that: owners of older federally assisted housing would have had to test for lead hazards before a family with a child under six moved in, fix any hazards within 30 days, and let the family move out on an emergency basis with no waiting list or penalty if they didn't. It also set up a federal program, funded at $50 million, to pay for removing lead hazards in homes rented with housing vouchers, and required notices to families about lead risks and their fair-housing rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 6 living in, or moving into, federally assisted housing built before 1978 — mostly low-income households. The bill's own findings cite CDC data that about 590,000 children under 6 (2.5 percent) had elevated blood lead levels on average between 2011 and 2016, and that there is no safe level of lead exposure for a child.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an initial lead-hazard risk assessment — not just a visual check — before or shortly after a family with a child under 6 occupies covered federally assisted housing built before 1978, and requires hazards found to be controlled within 30 days with notice to all residents.
Lets a family in housing where lead hazards were found but not fixed relocate on an emergency basis to another lead-safe unit with no waiting list, no penalty, and no gap in assistance.

Creates a six-year HUD demonstration program, authorized at $50 million, in which HUD pays to abate lead hazards found in voucher-rented homes where a child under 6 will live, with monitoring and public reporting on landlord participation and any fair-housing discrimination.
Requires written notice to families with young children about lead dangers, their fair-housing rights, and Medicaid's requirement of blood lead screening tests at ages 12 and 24 months.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, owners of federally assisted housing would bear the cost of the initial risk assessments, and taxpayers would fund the abatement program and related administrative costs — the bill authorizes $50 million for fiscal years 2023 through 2027 and conditions the new owner duties on Congress providing the money in advance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Older federally assisted landlords and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill itself acknowledges a real risk: it cites a lawsuit by the Massachusetts Fair Housing Center arguing that a similar pre-occupancy testing policy led to more housing discrimination against families with young children, making housing harder to find for exactly the families it aims to protect. The bill responds with notice requirements, anti-discrimination monitoring, and an exception for owners who offer a comparable lead-free unit, but the risk is not eliminated.

Owners of covered housing would carry the cost and time of risk assessments and, where funding is short, of controlling hazards — costs that could discourage participation in assisted housing programs. The bill limits this by requiring advance appropriations and by having HUD pay abatement costs in the voucher demonstration.

The federal spending is real: $50 million is authorized for the demonstration program alone, plus unspecified sums for agency compliance costs, assessor training, fair-housing enforcement, and a study of a national lead-removal strategy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — keeping lead out of the homes of young children before they are poisoned, rather than reacting after a diagnosis — is significant and one-way: lead exposure at low levels causes permanent cognitive and developmental harm, and the bill's duties would fall on a small, federally subsidized segment of the housing stock with federal money available for abatement. The honest concerns are the compliance burden on owners and the possibility that testing requirements make some landlords reluctant to rent to families with small children, which the bill tries to counter but cannot fully rule out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Donald McEachin introduced the Lead-Safe Housing for Kids Act of 2022 on March 18, 2022, joined by Representatives Pressley and Jesus Garcia of Illinois.
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the committee reporting the bill or the House voting on it, so the bill is dead and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never took effect, owners of older federally assisted housing never faced the new assessment and hazard-control duties, and no federal abatement money flowed. Nothing changed for children in assisted housing: the rule that a hazard assessment generally happens only after a child is diagnosed with lead poisoning remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of assisted housing; nothing changed for families

for.name: Reps. Ayanna Pressley and Jesús García
2 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — after the March 18, 2022 referral, and the bill died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition was recorded; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, but the record shows no position from Republicans or from the committee's leadership.

industries.industry: Owners of federally assisted housing built before 1978
industries.note: They would have had to conduct lead-hazard risk assessments and control hazards within 30 days, and cover the assessment cost in the voucher program — but abatement costs would be paid by HUD and the new duties would apply only after Congress provided money in advance. The burden is real but would have been paired with federally funded cleanup.

industries.industry: Lead risk assessment and abatement contractors
industries.note: The bill mandates risk assessments (explicitly beyond visual checks, adding dust, soil, paint, and water testing) and funds abatement, expanding paid work for certified assessors and abatement firms.

industries.industry: Public housing agencies and HUD grantees
industries.note: They would have gained federal money for compliance, testing, training, and outreach, but also taken on new assessment, notice, and relocation obligations.
